paragraphs: When one begins "Yotzer Or," he should touch the tefillin shel yad (hand-tefillin) alone, because the Yotzer blessing corresponds to the World of Beriah, and the tefillin shel yad also corresponds to the World of Beriah, and he should not do as the custom of the unlearned who also touch the tefillin shel rosh (head-tefillin), for touching the tefillin shel rosh has no place here — its place is before the Amidah, as we shall explain. And I found it written in a manuscript: it is good to keep one's hands upon the tefillin shel yad, over one's garments, for the entire duration of the blessings of the Shema recitation of Yotzer, so as to fulfill one's obligation regarding a lapse of attention, at least at this time — for there are those who hold that this suffices, so far. And this is indeed a sound counsel and a worthy practice; however, one who follows this practice should be careful to kiss [the tefillin] several times in the middle — that is, he should place his fingers on his lips and return them — for otherwise, once he has grown accustomed to keeping his hands on the tefillin shel yad, he may likewise doze off into a lapse of attention even in this, since the habit will become second nature and his mind will wander, and it will turn out that his practice did not help him.

clarification.explanation: At the start of the blessing "Yotzer Or," one should touch only the tefillin shel yad, since the Yotzer prayer belongs (by the esoteric tradition) to the World of Beriah, and the tefillin shel yad likewise belong to the World of Beriah — unlike the common practice of the masses, who also touch the tefillin shel rosh, whose place is before the Amidah (as will be explained). He found it written that it is good to keep one's hand on the tefillin shel yad, over the garment, throughout the blessings of the Shema recitation of Yotzer, in order to fulfill one's obligation despite a lapse of attention (some hold this suffices). One who follows this practice should be careful to kiss the fingers (which touched the tefillin) several times in the middle, lest the habit lull him and cause a complete lapse of attention.
takeaways: During the blessing of Yotzer Or, one touches only the tefillin shel yad (which corresponds to the same World of Beriah), not the tefillin shel rosh.
It is good to keep a hand on the tefillin throughout the blessings to prevent a lapse of attention, and to kiss the fingers occasionally so that the habit itself does not cause a lapse of attention.

paragraphs: The Kedushah of Yotzer must be said while seated, and if one was standing, he must sit; and the custom in our towns is that the congregation waits for the cantor here so that all may say the Kedushah of Yotzer together, and when they say the Kedushah of Yotzer, they also kiss the tefillin shel yad alone.

clarification.explanation: The Kedushah of "Yotzer" must be said while seated, and one who is standing must sit down. The custom in Baghdad is that the congregation waits for the cantor in order to say it together, and while saying it they also kiss the tefillin shel yad.
takeaways: The Kedushah of Yotzer is recited while seated, together with the congregation and the cantor, while kissing the tefillin shel yad.

paragraphs: One should pause between "Yotzer" and "Or" so that it not sound like "yitzror," as mentioned by the later authorities, and one must say "u'vtuvo mechadesh" ("and in His goodness renews") etc., because it is through the attribute of chesed, called "tov" ("good"), that renewal occurs, by the mystery of "they are new every morning" (Lamentations 3:23). One must also say "retzon koneihem" ("the will of their Maker"). One must also say "kedushah" with a shuruk vowel, [and] "kulam ke-echad" ("all of them as one") respond — referring back to "kulam ke-echad," meaning: Kedushah — all of them as one respond; therefore one should pause between the word "u'vin'imah" and the word "kedushah." One must also say "le'umat ha-serafim le'umatam meshabechim ve-omrim" as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. Also, in "la'El baruch ne'imut," the lamed should have a kamatz vowel, meaning: to the God who is known to be blessed, they give sweetness; and likewise "lemelech El chai ve-kayam" — the lamed of "lemelech" with a kamatz. Also, "v'tishbachot yashmi'u" — the tav is vowelized with a chirik, as I wrote above regarding Baruch She'amar, as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. "Umvarchin u'meshabchin" etc. — all begin with a vav and end with a nun. And when he says "ba'al gevurot," he should stress the ayin so that it not be swallowed and sound as if he were saying "bal gevurot" ("no might"), God forbid, as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim. And he should not say "lema'an lo neivosh" but rather say "v'lo neivosh v'lo nikalem," as mentioned by the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: One must pause between "Yotzer" and "Or" so that it not be heard as "yitzror." One says "u'vtuvo mechadesh" — because through the attribute of chesed (called "tov") the Creation is renewed every day (by the mystery of "new every morning"). Likewise one must say "retzon koneihem," vowelize "kedushah" with a shuruk, and pause before this word so that "all of them as one respond Kedushah" is heard correctly. There are several further precise vocalizations and textual points ("la'El baruch," "lemelech El chai ve-kayam," "v'tishbachot yashmi'u," the stress on the ayin in "ba'al gevurot" so it not sound like "bal gevurot" God forbid), and one should not say "lema'an lo neivosh" but rather "v'lo neivosh v'lo nikalem."
takeaways: One must pause correctly between words (Yotzer/Or, u'vin'imah/kedushah) so the meaning is not distorted.
Precise vocalizations matter (lemelech with a kamatz, ba'al gevurot with the stress) and the text "v'lo neivosh v'lo nikalem."

paragraphs: One who finds himself at "hagadol vehagibor" and is uncertain whether it refers to "shem kodshecha hagadol hagibor vehanora batachnu" or to "hagibor vehanora kadosh hu" of the blessing of Yotzer, should not go back to the first blessing, but rather go back to the blessing of Ahavat Olam and begin again from the beginning of "Ahavat," on account of a doubt regarding blessings, to be lenient.

clarification.explanation: One who finds himself saying "hagadol vehagibor" and is uncertain whether he is at the point where one says "shem kodshecha hagadol hagibor vehanora batachnu" (in the first blessings of Shema) or at "hagibor vehanora kadosh hu" (in the blessing of Yotzer) — should not go back to the first blessing but rather to the blessing of "Ahavat Olam," and begin again from "Ahavat," on account of a doubt regarding blessings, to be lenient.
takeaways: When in doubt as to where one is between the blessings, one goes back only to the beginning of "Ahavat Olam," not further.

paragraphs: When he says "maher v'haba aleinu," he should place both sides of the tallit upon his shoulders, and when he says "berachah v'shalom meherah me'arba kanfot kol ha'aretz," he should gather all four corners of the tallit and hold them in his left hand opposite the heart, which is on the left, and he should continue doing so until he says "u'devarav chayim v'kayamim v'ne'emanim" etc., which comes after "Emet v'Yatziv," as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. And in the book Keshet Gibor by the Gaon the Chida z"l, and other later authorities, it is written that he should place the tzitzit between the ring finger and the little finger, but this is not found explicitly stated in Sefer HaKavanot. And when he says "u'vno bacharta mikol am v'lashon v'keravtanu malkeinu," he should intend to fulfill the positive commandment of remembering the standing at Mount Sinai and the giving of the Torah, whereby the Blessed Name drew us near to His great Name through the Torah, and we accepted His kingship upon ourselves. And when he says "leshimcha hagadol," he should intend to fulfill the positive commandment of remembering the deed of Amalek, on whose account the Name is not whole and the Throne is not whole, and he should intend to look forward to the Lord that soon He will blot out the name of Amalek and His Blessed Name will become great, so that the Name and the Throne shall be made complete. And when he says "b'ahavah lehodot lecha," he should intend to fulfill the positive commandment of remembering what the Holy One, blessed be He, did to Miriam, for the Blessed Name did not create the mouth for man except to give thanks with it, and he should not use it for a forbidden matter. And in the verse "asher hotzeti etchem me'eretz Mitzrayim," he should intend to fulfill the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt, as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot and Peri Etz Chaim.

clarification.explanation: When saying "maher v'haba aleinu" he should place both sides of the tallit on his shoulders, and when saying "berachah v'shalom meherah me'arba kanfot kol ha'aretz" he should gather the four corners of the tallit and hold them in his left hand opposite the heart, continuing thus until "u'devarav chayim v'kayamim v'ne'emanim" (which follows "Emet v'Yatziv"). The author of Keshet Gibor (the Chida) and other later authorities wrote that one should place the tzitzit between the ring finger and the little finger, although this is not stated explicitly in Sefer HaKavanot. In the verses "u'vno bacharta... v'keravtanu malkeinu" one should intend to remember the standing at Sinai; in "leshimcha hagadol" — to remember the deed of Amalek (on whose account the Name and the Throne are not whole, and one looks forward to Amalek's name being blotted out and the Name made complete); in "b'ahavah lehodot lecha" — to remember what happened to Miriam (since the mouth was created for giving thanks alone); and in the verse "asher hotzeti etchem me'eretz Mitzrayim" — to remember the Exodus from Egypt.
takeaways: At certain verses one holds the corners of the tallit and intends specific remembrances (Sinai, Amalek, Miriam, the Exodus) — fulfilling four commandments of remembrance.

The author of Keshet Gibor (the Chida) and other later authorities wrote to place the tzitzit between the ring finger and little finger while holding them, although this is not stated explicitly in Sefer HaKavanot.

paragraphs: If one is in the middle of the blessings of the Shema and he is called up to the Torah by his name, I have shown, with Heaven's help, in my holy work Rav Pe'alim, that since he was called by his name he should go up and read along with the cantor in a whisper, and he should not stop to speak with the cantor regarding a charitable pledge or the like. And if he was called in the middle of the blessing "la'El ne'imut" or in the middle of "Ahavat Olam," then when he comes down he should go back and read from the beginning of that blessing; but only in the first blessing of Yotzer Or he should not go back to the beginning of the blessing, because it contains a mention of the Name, but rather he should go back to the beginning of the topic, so that matters be properly ordered. Also, during the blessings of the Shema he pauses to answer Kaddish or "Baruch Hashem hamevorach," whether for the Kaddish response or for the blessing said upon an aliyah to the Torah, and likewise he answers in the Kedushah the verse "Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" and the verse "Baruch," and likewise specifically the three words "Modim anachnu lach," and likewise the first five responses of Kaddish; but the other responses of "titkabel" and "al Yisrael" and "yehei shlama" he does not answer, and likewise the Amen of blessings, even the Amen of "ha'El hakadosh" and the Amen of "shome'a tefillah," he does not answer — even though, according to Maran z"l, one answers Kaddish up to "yitbarach," I have already proven in my holy work Makabtzi'el, following the view of our teacher the Ari zatzal, that one answers up to "be'alma," and this is the primary ruling, as I wrote above (Parashat Vayigash, item 9) in the laws of "Baruch She'amar." And although we said that one pauses during the blessings of the Shema for Kaddish and Kedushah etc., nevertheless, if he is at the beginning of a blessing, after having said "Baruch atah Hashem Eloheinu melech ha'olam," he should not pause for anything before saying "Yotzer Or u'vorei choshech," as is the law regarding the short blessings of enjoyment or of commandments, in which one does not pause at all — for if he were to pause, the blessing would become mixed with words of no relevance immediately after the mention of the Name. And so here, how could he say "Baruch atah Hashem Eloheinu melech ha'olam, Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh" etc., or "Baruch atah Hashem Eloheinu melech ha'olam, Amen yehei shmei raba" etc.? And so with the other responses of "Baruch" and of "Modim" and the Amen of Kaddish, as the Rav Nishmat Kol Chai wrote, Part 1, Siman 2; and the same law applies to the blessing of "Baruch She'amar" after one has begun the blessing, as I wrote above.

clarification.explanation: One who is called up to the Torah by his own name in the middle of the blessings of the Shema should go up and read along with the cantor in a whisper, and should not stop to speak with the cantor (for instance, about a charitable pledge). If he was called up in the middle of "la'El baruch ne'imut" or "Ahavat Olam," then when he comes down he goes back to the beginning of that blessing; but for the first blessing of "Yotzer Or" (which contains a mention of the Name), he does not go back to its beginning but rather to the beginning of the topic, so that things remain in proper order. Likewise, one pauses in the middle of the blessings of the Shema to answer Kaddish, Barechu, Kedushah ("Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh," "Baruch"), and "Modim anachnu lach" only, and the first five responses of Kaddish — but not the other responses (of "titkabel," "al Yisrael," "yehei shlama") nor the Amen of blessings (such as "ha'El hakadosh," "shome'a tefillah"). And regarding the Kaddish response itself — one answers up to "be'alma," and this is the primary ruling (not up to "yitbarach" as Maran held). However, at the beginning of any blessing, after saying "Baruch atah Hashem Eloheinu melech ha'olam" and before completing the actual blessing (such as "Yotzer Or u'vorei choshech") — one does not pause for anything, as is the law for short blessings.
takeaways: One called to the Torah in the middle of the blessings of the Shema goes up and reads in a whisper with the cantor; for the first blessing he returns to the beginning of the topic, for the others to the beginning of the blessing.

In the middle of the blessings, one answers Kaddish (up to "be'alma"), Kedushah, Modim, and the first five responses — but not immediately after opening a blessing ("Baruch atah Hashem") before its completion.

paragraphs: Regarding the fifteen vavs of "Emet v'Yatziv" etc., one should be careful to pronounce them with the mouth very precisely, because they contain a mystical secret, and one must connect the word "hadavar" to the fifteen vavs mentioned without pausing between them, because the letter heh of "hadavar" belongs to them. And in my holy work Makabtzi'el I have shown, with Heaven's help, that if one happens to need to answer something of the matters of holiness that are answered within the blessings of the Shema, he should answer even in the middle of the fifteen vavs mentioned, except that he must then go back and say "v'yatziv" etc., in order to connect the fifteen vavs mentioned to the heh of "hadavar" without any interruption by another matter in between.

clarification.explanation: In the fifteen "vavs" of "Emet v'Yatziv" (which contain a mystical secret) one must pronounce them very precisely, and connect the word "hadavar" to them without pause (the heh of "hadavar" belongs to them). If one happens to need to answer a matter of holiness in their midst, he should answer there as well, but must go back and say "v'yatziv" etc. in order to connect the vavs to "hadavar" without interruption.
takeaways: The fifteen vavs of "Emet v'Yatziv" (which contain a secret) are pronounced precisely and connected to "hadavar" without pause; if one answered something, he goes back and reconnects them.

paragraphs: When he says "u'devarav chayim v'kayamim v'nechmadim la'ad," then at the word "la'ad" he should kiss the tzitzit that he had been holding and pass them over his eyes, and then release them from his hand so that they fall down, and he should not hold them in his hand any longer, as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. And one must say "yotzreinu tzur yeshu'ateinu" and not say "tzureinu." And likewise "lemelech El chai v'kayam" — he should say the first lamed of "lamelech" with a kamatz and not with a sheva, as mentioned above (item 3) regarding "la'El baruch." Also, one should say "ram v'nisa gadol v'nora" and not say "gibor v'nora," as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. And when he says "ozer dalim," he should intend to make himself poor together with the Shechinah, which is called "dalah" ("poor"), in that she is below in the Palace of the Will of Beriah, so that when she ascends he too may merit an elevation of his soul along with her; and this intention is alluded to in the holy Zohar, which said: "one must make himself poor together with the Shechinah," as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. And when he says "tehilot la'El elyon go'alam," he should rise and stand before the Supreme King, blessed be He, and remain standing until the end of the Amidah, as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot; and I have written in my holy work Makabtzi'el that immediately at the beginning of the word "tehilot" he should rise to stand and finish the word "tehilot" while standing — see the Siddur of our teacher the Rashash z"l.

clarification.explanation: When saying "u'devarav chayim v'kayamim v'nechmadim la'ad," at the word "la'ad" he should kiss the tzitzit he was holding, pass them over his eyes, and then release them from his hand so they fall down. One must say "yotzreinu tzur yeshu'ateinu" (not "tzureinu"), "lemelech El chai v'kayam" with a kamatz, and "ram v'nisa gadol v'nora" (not "gibor v'nora"). When saying "ozer dalim" he should intend to join in the poverty of the Shechinah, called "dalah" (per the Zohar: "one must make himself poor together with the Shechinah"), and when saying "tehilot la'El elyon go'alam" he should rise to stand before the Supreme King and remain standing until the end of the Amidah.
takeaways: At "la'ad" one kisses the tzitzit and passes them over the eyes; there are further precise textual points (yotzreinu, lemelech with a kamatz, ram v'nisa).
At "ozer dalim" one intends to join in the (mystical) poverty of the Shechinah; at "tehilot la'El elyon go'alam" one rises and remains standing until the end of the Amidah.

paragraphs: One must juxtapose redemption to prayer, and must not pause after saying "ga'al Yisrael" even in silence, but rather he should immediately begin saying "Adonai sefatai tiftach." And if he sensed that they wish to say Kaddish or Kedushah, he should wait before saying "shirah chadashah" and answer there; but after he has said "ga'al Yisrael," he should not pause for Kaddish or Kedushah or for anything of the matters of holiness mentioned above. And if a Torah scroll is raised to show the congregation, he should not wait to look at the Torah scroll, even in silence, after he has said "ga'al Yisrael," for there is a mystical secret in this matter of juxtaposing redemption to prayer. And for this reason our Sages did not institute saying Kaddish between the Yotzer prayer, which is in the World of Beriah, and the Amidah prayer, which is in Atzilut, even though they instituted Kaddish between every world and the next, as we explained above (Parashat Vayechi, item 1). And there is yet another reason for this matter, according to the mystical tradition, why it was not necessary to institute Kaddish at this point: because there is no need to say Kaddish here in order to raise up the Beriah into the World of Atzilut, since without this it is already entirely bound up with the Malchut of Atzilut, as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot.

clarification.explanation: One must juxtapose redemption to prayer: after "ga'al Yisrael" he must not pause even in silence, but must immediately say "Adonai sefatai tiftach." If they wish to say Kaddish or Kedushah at that moment, he should wait and refrain from saying "shirah chadashah" (the verse before "ga'al Yisrael") until he answers there; but after he has said "ga'al Yisrael" itself, he must not pause any longer for anything of holiness, and even if a Torah scroll is raised to show it, he should not wait to look at it even in silence. There is a deep secret in this (the juxtaposition of redemption to prayer), and for this same reason the Sages did not institute Kaddish between the Yotzer prayer (World of Beriah) and the Amidah (World of Atzilut), even though they instituted Kaddish between the other worlds — because the Beriah here is already entirely bound up with the Malchut of Atzilut without need for an elevating Kaddish.
takeaways: After "ga'al Yisrael" one must not pause for anything (even silence or looking at a Torah scroll) — this is the juxtaposition of redemption to prayer.
The inner reason: there is no Kaddish between Yotzer and the Amidah, because the Beriah here is already directly bound up with Atzilut.
